items.stem: Which apparatus measures 25.0 cm³ of solution most accurately?
items.answer: volumetric pipette
items.markingKey: A pipette delivers a fixed volume accurately (±0.05 cm³).

items.stem: Which apparatus is used to measure the volume of gas produced in a reaction?
items.answer: gas syringe
items.markingKey: A gas syringe (or inverted measuring cylinder/burette over water).

items.stem: Explain why a burette is used rather than a measuring cylinder to add acid in a titration.
items.answer: A burette measures variable volumes much more precisely (to 0.05 cm³) and allows drop-by-drop addition near the end-point.

items.stem: In a titration, the initial burette reading is 0.00 cm³ and the final reading is 20.75 cm³. Calculate the titre and state the precision to which burette readings are recorded.
items.answer: 20.75 cm³; to the nearest 0.05 cm³

items.stem: Samuel investigates the reaction of magnesium ribbon with dilute hydrochloric acid by measuring the volume of hydrogen produced every 20 s. Results (time / s, volume / cm³): 0, 0; 20, 26; 40, 40; 60, 49; 80, 53; 100, 56. (a) Name the apparatus used to measure the volume of gas. (b) Name the apparatus used to measure time. (c) Suggest why the results become less reliable if the bung is not inserted quickly.
items.answer: (a) Gas syringe. (b) Stop-watch. (c) Some gas escapes before it can be collected, so readings are too low.

items.stem: To what precision is a burette normally read?
items.answer: to the nearest 0.05 cm³
items.markingKey: Burette readings are recorded to two decimal places, ending in 0 or 5.

items.stem: Explain why it is good practice to repeat measurements.
items.answer: To identify anomalous results and calculate a reliable mean.

items.stem: Explain why a thermometer reading 0.1 °C intervals is better than one reading 1 °C intervals when measuring a temperature rise of 3 °C.
items.answer: The smaller scale division gives a smaller relative uncertainty, so the temperature change is more accurate.

items.stem: Three titres from a titration are 20.75 cm³, 21.55 cm³ and 20.70 cm³. Identify the concordant titres, calculate the mean titre, and explain why the other result is not used.
items.answer: 20.75 and 20.70; mean 20.73 cm³; 21.55 cm³ differs by more than 0.10 cm³ (anomalous).
items.markingKey: 1 mark concordant pair; 1 mark mean; 1 mark reason [3]

items.stem: Hana investigates the reaction of marble chips (calcium carbonate) with dilute hydrochloric acid by measuring the volume of carbon dioxide produced every 20 s. Results (time / s, volume / cm³): 0, 0; 20, 42; 40, 63; 60, 74; 80, 79; 100, 81. (a) Name the apparatus used to measure the volume of gas. (b) State and explain how the rate changes during the experiment. (c) Identify one variable that must be controlled.
items.answer: (a) Gas syringe. (b) Rate decreases: the concentration of acid (and amount of solid) falls, so collisions are less frequent. (c) Temperature, concentration/volume of acid, or mass/surface area of the solid.

items.stem: What is a saturated solution?
options: A solution containing the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve at that temperature
A solution that contains no solute
items.answer: A solution containing the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve at that temperature
items.markingKey: No more solute dissolves at that temperature.

items.stem: Explain why crystals form when a hot saturated solution of potassium nitrate is cooled.
items.answer: Solubility decreases as temperature falls, so the solution can hold less solute and the excess crystallises out.

items.stem: Explain why simple distillation cannot separate ethanol from water efficiently.
items.answer: Their boiling points are close, so both evaporate; a fractionating column is needed to separate them.

items.stem: Solubility of copper(II) sulfate in g per 100 g of water — 20 °C: 32 g; 40 °C: 45 g; 60 °C: 62 g; 80 °C: 84 g. Calculate the mass of copper(II) sulfate that crystallises when a saturated solution in 200 g of water is cooled from 40 °C to 20 °C.

Solubility of potassium nitrate in g per 100 g of water — 20 °C: 32 g; 40 °C: 64 g; 60 °C: 110 g; 80 °C: 169 g. Calculate the mass of potassium nitrate that crystallises when a saturated solution in 100 g of water is cooled from 80 °C to 20 °C. Describe how the crystals are then separated from the solution and dried.
items.answer: 137 g; filter, wash with a little cold distilled water and dry between filter papers (or in a warm oven).
items.markingKey: difference = 169 − 32 = 137 g per 100 g [1]; × 100/100 = 137 g [1]; filter, wash and dry [1]

items.stem: Lucas is given a solution of ethanol, water and a dissolved coloured dye and asked to obtain pure samples of the components. (a) Describe a method to separate the components. (b) Describe how you could show that the water collected is pure.
items.answer: (a) fractional distillation to collect ethanol at 78 °C; then water at 100 °C; dye left in flask; check purity by chromatography. (b) Measure its boiling point: 100 °C exactly (or freezing point 0 °C).

items.stem: In salt solution, what is the solvent?
items.answer: water
items.markingKey: Solvent = the liquid that dissolves the solute (salt).

items.stem: Explain the difference between dissolving and melting.
items.answer: Dissolving: solute particles spread among solvent particles to form a solution; melting: a solid turns into a liquid on heating — one substance only.

items.stem: Explain why salt cannot be removed from sea water by filtration.
items.answer: The salt is dissolved; its particles pass through the filter paper with the water.

items.stem: Iodine dissolves in ethanol to form iodine solution. What is the solvent?
items.answer: ethanol
items.markingKey: solute iodine; solvent ethanol; solution iodine solution.

items.stem: Solubility of potassium nitrate in g per 100 g of water — 20 °C: 32 g; 40 °C: 64 g; 60 °C: 110 g; 80 °C: 169 g. Calculate the mass of potassium nitrate that crystallises when a saturated solution in 25 g of water is cooled from 80 °C to 20 °C.
Sulfur dissolves in methylbenzene to form sulfur solution. What is the solute?
items.answer: sulfur
items.markingKey: solute sulfur; solvent methylbenzene; solution sulfur solution.

items.stem: A technician in Istanbul must separate a mixture of copper(II) oxide powder and copper(II) sulfate crystals. (a) Define the terms solute and solvent. (b) Explain why the filtrate is not evaporated to dryness when making crystals. (c) Describe how you could show that the water collected is pure.
items.answer: (a) Solute: substance that dissolves; solvent: liquid in which it dissolves. (b) Crystals would be small/impure and lose water of crystallisation; heat to saturation and cool instead. (c) Measure its boiling point: 100 °C exactly (or freezing point 0 °C).

items.stem: In simple distillation, where should the thermometer bulb be placed?
options: next to the side-arm leading to the condenser
at the bottom of the condenser
items.answer: next to the side-arm leading to the condenser
items.markingKey: It measures the temperature of the vapour entering the condenser.

items.stem: Explain why anti-bumping granules are added to the flask during distillation.
items.answer: They give smooth boiling and prevent large bubbles forming suddenly (bumping).

items.stem: Explain how simple distillation obtains pure water from salt solution.
items.answer: Water boils and its vapour passes into the condenser, where it cools and condenses; salt has a very high boiling point so stays in the flask.

items.stem: A mixture of hexane (b.p. 69 °C) and ethanoic acid (b.p. 118 °C) is separated by fractional distillation. State which liquid is collected first, the thermometer reading while it distils, and how you would know when the second liquid starts to distil.
items.answer: hexane first, at 69 °C; the temperature rises again and stays constant at 118 °C when ethanoic acid distils.
items.markingKey: 1 mark first liquid; 1 mark temperature; 1 mark sign of second fraction [3]

items.stem: A mixture of butan-1-ol (b.p. 117 °C) and propan-1-ol (b.p. 97 °C) is separated by fractional distillation. State which liquid is collected first, the thermometer reading while it distils, and how you would know when the second liquid starts to distil.
items.answer: propan-1-ol first, at 97 °C; the temperature rises again and stays constant at 117 °C when butan-1-ol distils.
items.markingKey: 1 mark first liquid; 1 mark temperature; 1 mark sign of second fraction [3]

items.stem: A mixture of cyclohexane (b.p. 81 °C) and propan-1-ol (b.p. 97 °C) is separated by fractional distillation. State which liquid is collected first, the thermometer reading while it distils, and how you would know when the second liquid starts to distil.
items.answer: cyclohexane first, at 81 °C; the temperature rises again and stays constant at 97 °C when propan-1-ol distils.
items.markingKey: 1 mark first liquid; 1 mark temperature; 1 mark sign of second fraction [3]

items.stem: A perfume company in Auckland purifies cyclohexane from a mixture with butan-1-ol. (a) State which liquid is collected first and the thermometer reading. (b) State one safety precaution. (c) Name one industrial process that uses fractional distillation.
items.answer: (a) cyclohexane at 81 °C (b) Heat with a water bath/electric heater if flammable; do not heat to dryness; use anti-bumping granules; goggles. (c) Separating crude oil into fractions (or liquid air).

items.stem: A diagram shows a flask containing propan-1-ol and methanol, a fractionating column, a thermometer, a condenser and a receiver. (a) Explain why fractional distillation, rather than simple distillation, is used. (b) State which liquid is collected first and the thermometer reading. (c) State one safety precaution.
items.answer: (a) The liquids are miscible with boiling points fairly close together; the column gives better separation. (b) methanol at 65 °C (c) Heat with a water bath/electric heater if flammable; do not heat to dryness; use anti-bumping granules; goggles.

items.stem: Why does cold water enter the condenser at the bottom?
options: So that the condenser fills completely and cools efficiently
To make the vapour flow faster
items.answer: So that the condenser fills completely and cools efficiently
items.markingKey: Counter-current flow keeps the jacket full.

items.stem: Explain why a water bath is used instead of a Bunsen flame when distilling ethanol.
items.answer: Ethanol is flammable; a water bath heats gently without a naked flame and to below 100 °C.

items.stem: Explain why the temperature at the top of the fractionating column stays constant while a fraction is being collected.
items.answer: Only one pure substance is reaching the thermometer, so the temperature equals its boiling point.

items.stem: During a separation, Ana placed the thermometer bulb in the boiling liquid during distillation. Explain what is wrong and how to correct it.
items.answer: It reads the liquid temperature, not the vapour; place it at the side-arm.

items.stem: A mixture of ethanol (b.p. 78 °C) and hexane (b.p. 69 °C) is separated by fractional distillation. State which liquid is collected first, the thermometer reading while it distils, and how you would know when the second liquid starts to distil.
items.answer: hexane first, at 69 °C; the temperature rises again and stays constant at 78 °C when ethanol distils.
items.markingKey: 1 mark first liquid; 1 mark temperature; 1 mark sign of second fraction [3]

items.stem: Describe how you would obtain solid barium sulfate from a reaction mixture using filtration. Name the key apparatus.
items.answer: Filtration (separating an insoluble solid from a liquid): filter funnel; filter paper; conical flask or beaker.

items.stem: A mixture of ethanol (b.p. 78 °C) and ethanoic acid (b.p. 118 °C) is separated by fractional distillation. State which liquid is collected first, the thermometer reading while it distils, and how you would know when the second liquid starts to distil.
items.answer: ethanol first, at 78 °C; the temperature rises again and stays constant at 118 °C when ethanoic acid distils.
items.markingKey: 1 mark first liquid; 1 mark temperature; 1 mark sign of second fraction [3]

items.stem: Describe how you would obtain pure water from tap water using simple distillation. Name the key apparatus.
items.answer: Simple distillation (separating a solvent from a solution): distillation flask; thermometer at the side-arm; Liebig condenser with water in at the bottom.

items.stem: Describe how you would separate ethanol from a fermented mixture using fractional distillation. Name the key apparatus.
items.answer: Fractional distillation (separating miscible liquids with different boiling points): round-bottomed flask; fractionating column packed with glass beads; thermometer and condenser.

items.stem: A perfume company in Cape Town purifies methanol from a mixture with ethanol. (a) Explain why fractional distillation, rather than simple distillation, is used. (b) Describe what happens inside the fractionating column.
items.answer: (a) The liquids are miscible with boiling points fairly close together; the column gives better separation. (b) Vapours repeatedly condense and re-evaporate on the glass beads; the more volatile liquid rises to the top.

items.stem: A diagram shows a flask containing propan-1-ol and ethanoic acid, a fractionating column, a thermometer, a condenser and a receiver. (a) State which liquid is collected first and the thermometer reading. (b) Describe what happens inside the fractionating column.
items.answer: (a) propan-1-ol at 97 °C (b) Vapours repeatedly condense and re-evaporate on the glass beads; the more volatile liquid rises to the top.

items.stem: Why is the baseline on a chromatogram drawn in pencil rather than ink?
options: Ink would react with the paper
Pencil does not dissolve in the solvent
items.answer: Pencil does not dissolve in the solvent
items.markingKey: Ink would dissolve and move up the paper, confusing the results.

items.stem: Explain why different substances travel different distances on a chromatogram.
items.answer: They have different solubilities in the solvent and different attraction to the paper; more soluble substances travel further.

items.stem: Explain why a lid is placed on the beaker during chromatography.
items.answer: To keep the atmosphere saturated with solvent vapour so the solvent does not evaporate from the paper.

items.stem: A spot moved 3.8 cm from the baseline and the solvent front moved 7.5 cm. Calculate the Rf value.

In a chromatogram, an unknown dye moves 6.6 cm and the solvent front moves 11 cm. The Rf values of known dyes in the same solvent are: A 0.20, F 0.45, B 0.35. Calculate the Rf of the unknown and deduce which dye it could be.
items.answer: Rf = 0.60; it does not match any of the known dyes.
items.markingKey: 1 mark Rf; 1 mark matching conclusion; 1 mark same solvent/conditions [3]

items.stem: Lina uses paper chromatography to test a black ink. Known dyes blue, yellow, green are spotted next to the ink. The solvent front moves 12 cm. The ink gives two spots, at 8.4 cm and 7.2 cm; the known dyes travel blue 5.4 cm, yellow 8.4 cm, green 7.2 cm. (a) Identify the dyes present in the ink. (b) Explain why the solvent level must be below the baseline. (c) Suggest why the Rf values must be compared using the same solvent.
items.answer: (a) yellow and green (b) Otherwise the spots dissolve into the solvent in the beaker. (c) Rf values depend on the solvent (and temperature/paper).

items.stem: Explain why an Rf value is always less than 1.
items.answer: The substance cannot travel further than the solvent front.

items.stem: Explain why the purity of substances such as drugs and foods is important.
items.answer: Impurities could be harmful/toxic or reduce effectiveness.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why the purity of substances such as drugs and foods is important. (b) Explain why different substances travel different distances on a chromatogram.
items.answer: (a) Impurities could be harmful/toxic or reduce effectiveness. (b) They have different solubilities in the solvent and different attraction to the paper; more soluble substances travel further.

items.stem: Pure vanillin melts at 82 °C. A sample made by Zara melts sharply at 82 °C. Deduce whether the sample is pure and explain your answer.
items.answer: Pure: it has a sharp melting point equal to the data value.

items.stem: Pure salicylic acid melts at 159 °C. A sample made by Lina melts sharply at 159 °C. Deduce whether the sample is pure and explain your answer.
items.answer: Pure: it has a sharp melting point equal to the data value.

items.stem: Amara uses paper chromatography to test a black ink. Known dyes yellow, orange, red are spotted next to the ink. The solvent front moves 10 cm. The ink gives two spots, at 2.5 cm and 7.0 cm; the known dyes travel yellow 7.0 cm, orange 3.5 cm, red 2.5 cm. (a) Calculate the Rf values of the two spots in the ink. (b) Describe how a colourless amino acid could be seen on a chromatogram.
items.answer: (a) 0.25 and 0.70 (b) Dry the paper and spray with a locating agent; spots become visible.

items.stem: Omar uses paper chromatography to test a black ink. Known dyes blue, red, green are spotted next to the ink. The solvent front moves 12 cm. The ink gives two spots, at 5.4 cm and 3.0 cm; the known dyes travel blue 5.4 cm, red 3.0 cm, green 7.2 cm. (a) Calculate the Rf values of the two spots in the ink. (b) Identify the dyes present in the ink. (c) Explain why the baseline is drawn in pencil. (d) Explain why the solvent level must be below the baseline.
items.answer: (a) 0.45 and 0.25 (b) blue and red (c) Pencil is insoluble in the solvent and will not run. (d) Otherwise the spots dissolve into the solvent in the beaker.

items.stem: Which unit is used for volumes measured with a burette?
items.answer: cm³
items.markingKey: Laboratory volumes are given in cm³ (dm³ for larger volumes).

items.stem: Explain why the mass of a reaction flask is recorded as soon as the reactants are mixed in a rate experiment.
items.answer: Gas begins escaping immediately, so a late reading would be too low and the initial mass would be wrong.

items.stem: In an experiment the starting temperature was 18.5 °C and the highest temperature reached was 33.5 °C. Calculate the temperature change and state whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic. Suggest one improvement to the apparatus to reduce heat loss.
items.answer: +15.0 °C; exothermic; use an insulated (polystyrene) cup with a lid.
items.markingKey: 1 mark change; 1 mark type; 1 mark improvement [3]

items.stem: Ethan investigates the reaction of marble chips (calcium carbonate) with dilute hydrochloric acid by measuring the volume of carbon dioxide produced every 20 s. Results (time / s, volume / cm³): 0, 0; 20, 22; 40, 36; 60, 45; 80, 51; 100, 54. (a) Name the apparatus used to measure the volume of gas. (b) State and explain how the rate changes during the experiment. (c) Suggest how the volume of acid should be measured, and why. (d) Identify one variable that must be controlled. (e) Suggest why the results become less reliable if the bung is not inserted quickly.
items.answer: (a) Gas syringe. (b) Rate decreases: the concentration of acid (and amount of solid) falls, so collisions are less frequent. (c) Measuring cylinder is adequate (the acid is in excess) — or a pipette/burette for greater accuracy. (d) Temperature, concentration/volume of acid, or mass/surface area of the solid. (e) Some gas escapes before it can be collected, so readings are too low.

items.stem: The substance left on the filter paper after filtration is called the
items.answer: residue
items.markingKey: Residue stays in the paper; filtrate passes through.

items.stem: Suggest a method to obtain nitrogen and oxygen from liquid air and explain why it works.
items.answer: Fractional distillation: they have different boiling points.

items.stem: Copper(II) sulfate dissolves in water to form blue copper(II) sulfate solution. What is the solvent?
items.answer: water
items.markingKey: solute copper(II) sulfate; solvent water; solution blue copper(II) sulfate solution.

items.stem: A technician in Dhaka must separate a mixture of copper(II) oxide powder and copper(II) sulfate crystals. (a) Define the terms solute and solvent. (b) Describe how you could show that the water collected is pure.
items.answer: (a) Solute: substance that dissolves; solvent: liquid in which it dissolves. (b) Measure its boiling point: 100 °C exactly (or freezing point 0 °C).

items.stem: Daniel is given a mixture of sand, salt and water and asked to obtain pure samples of the components. (a) Explain why the filtrate is not evaporated to dryness when making crystals. items.answer: (a) Crystals would be small/impure and lose water of crystallisation; heat to saturation and cool instead. (b) One in which no more solute can dissolve at that temperature. (c) Measure its boiling point: 100 °C exactly (or freezing point 0 °C).

items.stem: Which separation technique uses evaporating basin?
items.answer: crystallisation
items.markingKey: crystallisation (obtaining a soluble solid from its solution) uses evaporating basin, Bunsen burner and tripod (or water bath), glass rod to test for the point of crystallisation.

items.stem: During a separation, Daniel placed the thermometer bulb in the boiling liquid during distillation. Explain what is wrong and how to correct it.
items.answer: It reads the liquid temperature, not the vapour; place it at the side-arm.

items.stem: Yusuf separates a mixture of cyclohexane and methanol using fractional distillation. (a) Describe what happens inside the fractionating column. (b) Explain why the water enters the condenser at the bottom. (c) Name one industrial process that uses fractional distillation.
items.answer: (a) Vapours repeatedly condense and re-evaporate on the glass beads; the more volatile liquid rises to the top. (b) The jacket stays full of cold water so cooling is efficient. (c) Separating crude oil into fractions (or liquid air).

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why different substances travel different distances on a chromatogram. (b) Explain why a lid is placed on the beaker during chromatography.
items.answer: (a) They have different solubilities in the solvent and different attraction to the paper; more soluble substances travel further. (b) To keep the atmosphere saturated with solvent vapour so the solvent does not evaporate from the paper.

items.stem: How should the volume in a measuring cylinder be read?
options: at the side of the cylinder
at the bottom of the meniscus with the eye level with it
at the top of the meniscus from above
items.answer: at the bottom of the meniscus with the eye level with it

items.stem: In a quality-control laboratory, Ravi used a measuring cylinder to find the volume of hydrogen collected over 10 s intervals. Explain why this is a poor technique and suggest an improvement.
items.answer: It is better to use a gas syringe, which gives a direct and more precise reading as gas is produced.

items.stem: In an experiment the starting temperature was 18.5 °C and the lowest temperature reached was 14.0 °C. Calculate the temperature change and state whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic. Suggest one improvement to the apparatus to reduce heat loss.

items.stem: Suggest a method to obtain chalk (calcium carbonate) from a suspension in water and explain why it works.
items.answer: Filtration: chalk is insoluble.

items.stem: Describe how you would obtain crystals of copper(II) sulfate from its solution using crystallisation. Name the key apparatus.
items.answer: Crystallisation (obtaining a soluble solid from its solution): evaporating basin; Bunsen burner and tripod (or water bath); glass rod to test for the point of crystallisation.

items.stem: Ethan separates a mixture of hexane and butan-1-ol using fractional distillation. (a) Describe what happens inside the fractionating column. (b) Suggest how the purity of the first fraction could be checked. (c) State one safety precaution.
items.answer: (a) Vapours repeatedly condense and re-evaporate on the glass beads; the more volatile liquid rises to the top. (b) Measure its boiling point: pure hexane boils sharply at 69 °C. (c) Heat with a water bath/electric heater if flammable; do not heat to dryness; use anti-bumping granules; goggles.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why a lid is placed on the beaker during chromatography. (b) Explain why different substances travel different distances on a chromatogram.
items.answer: (a) To keep the atmosphere saturated with solvent vapour so the solvent does not evaporate from the paper. (b) They have different solubilities in the solvent and different attraction to the paper; more soluble substances travel further.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why different substances travel different distances on a chromatogram. (b) Explain why an Rf value is always less than 1.
items.answer: (a) They have different solubilities in the solvent and different attraction to the paper; more soluble substances travel further. (b) The substance cannot travel further than the solvent front.

items.stem: Pure stearic acid melts at 69 °C. A sample made by Kenji melts over the range 65–68 °C. Deduce whether the sample is pure and explain your answer.
items.answer: Impure: impurities lower the melting point and make it melt over a range.

items.stem: In a chromatogram, an unknown dye moves 9.6 cm and the solvent front moves 12 cm. The Rf values of known dyes in the same solvent are: A 0.20, F 0.45, C 0.50. Calculate the Rf of the unknown and deduce which dye it could be.
items.answer: Rf = 0.80; it does not match any of the known dyes.
items.markingKey: 1 mark Rf; 1 mark matching conclusion; 1 mark same solvent/conditions [3]

items.stem: Sofia uses paper chromatography to test a black ink. Known dyes green, yellow, red are spotted next to the ink. The solvent front moves 10 cm. The ink gives two spots, at 7.0 cm and 6.0 cm; the known dyes travel green 6.0 cm, yellow 7.0 cm, red 2.5 cm. (a) Explain why the baseline is drawn in pencil. (b) Explain why the solvent level must be below the baseline. (c) Suggest why the Rf values must be compared using the same solvent. (d) Explain how chromatography separates the dyes.
items.answer: (a) Pencil is insoluble in the solvent and will not run. (b) Otherwise the spots dissolve into the solvent in the beaker. (c) Rf values depend on the solvent (and temperature/paper). (d) Dyes have different solubilities in the solvent/attractions to the paper so travel different distances.
